newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union picks GM as next target.
newsitem.headline: Canada union picks GM as next target.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers union president Buzz Hargrove said on Monday that the union chose General Motors Corp's Canadian unit as its next negotiating target, with a strike deadline of October 2.
"We have decided this morning that General Motors Corp is going to be the second target," Hargrove told a news conference.

Hargrove said he was certain the United Auto Workers in the United States would not pick GM as its next negotiating target after the ratification of the UAW's tentative agreement with Ford Motor Co was completed on September 29.

"We have a clear understanding between myself and Mr (Stephen) Yokich (president) of the UAW that we will not do anything to interfere or harm one another in our efforts to put together a 1996 collective agreement," Hargrove said.
Hargrove said he intended to press on GM Canada the terms of the CAW's newly ratified deal with Chrysler Canada and was determined to reverse GM's outsourcing decisions.
General Motors said earlier this year that it intended to sell two parts plants in Canada and outsource more than 5,000 unionized jobs.
"We're determined to reverse these decisions as we head to the bargaining table with GM," Hargrove said.
Hargrove was not optimistic about the prospects for reaching a deal without a strike at GM.

"We are looking for a settlement, but we are also preparing our members for a strike if that becomes necessary," Hargrove said. He warned GM Canada that the union was prepared for an extended strike to back its demands.

"We have scheduled a special convention for October 18 for the purpose of putting a special dues assesment on the total union if we're into a long protracted strike at General Motors, to ensure the largest section of our union would not be forced to be on the picket line without strike pay," Hargrove said.
He said the union could use the tactic of escalating strikes, by walking out of one plant after another as a strike wore on, rather than shutting down all the plants at once.
He said the union could eventually shut down all of GM's Canadian and possibly North American operations once all of its 28,510 GM workers were on the picket line.

GM endured a 17-day strike by the United Auto Workers over outsourcing at its Dayton, Ohio brake plant earlier this year, which shut down its entire North American operations and cost the carmaker about US$900 million.
GM Canada executives were not immediately available for comment.

The CAW last went on strike in Canada at Ford's subsidiary for nine days in 1990, but has held its longest strikes against GM. The Canadian union broke with the UAW in 1984 when it refused to accept concessions in a GM contract agreed to by the U.S. union.
